# What 850,000 mortgage decisions taught me about building a fair approval model

**Muhammad Sabeeh Ansari · LoanWise AI · case study** — every number below is regenerated by `python -m ml.run` into [`reports/ml/REPORT.md`](../reports/ml/REPORT.md).

> **In short:** I rebuilt a loan-approval model on 850,000 real US mortgage decisions, caught two data leaks along the way, and found that a model that is fairer *on average* can be far less fair *at its decision threshold*. That result replicated in five states. Then I shipped the model in a working app, with the gap disclosed rather than hidden.

## The problem with version 1

LoanWise v1 was a working product: a React and FastAPI app that scores an application, explains it with SHAP, audits fairness and has an LLM write the decision letter. The ML underneath was weak, though. It used 614 rows from a Kaggle dataset, credit history was a yes/no flag, and the currency was unclear. The fairness audit rested on **112 women**. Honest evaluation showed the model barely beat a one-line rule. The engineering was ahead of the evidence, so for v2 I replaced the data instead of tuning the model.

## Data and setup

- **Source:** public **HMDA** records, which US lenders must file for every mortgage application. I used home-purchase decisions only.
- **Main experiment:** trained on Georgia **2022** (151,421 applications) and tested once on Georgia **2023** (120,170). A time-based split is the honest test for a model that will meet next year's applicants.
- **Robustness:** Georgia **2021**, plus 2023 data from four states the model never saw: North Carolina, Ohio, Arizona and Washington. That's **852,883** applications in all.
- **Reproducibility:** downloads are pinned with SHA-256 checksums. Every scoping rule logs how many rows it removed. Operating thresholds are chosen on training-year out-of-fold predictions (each row scored by a model that never saw it), never on test data. The pipeline is a tested Python package (59 unit tests), not a notebook.

## Finding 1: two leaks, one obvious and one subtle

HMDA rows contain fields that only exist **after** the lender decides: the interest rate, closing costs and denial reasons. A model given them scores **ROC-AUC 1.000** (0.5 is a coin flip, 1.0 is perfect), which is meaningless. A missingness audit flags them automatically; `interest_rate`, for example, is blank for 100% of denials.

The second leak looked innocent. `preapproval` is known before any decision, yet **all 8,613 applications that requested one were approved**. Denied preapprovals are filed under a different action code, which my approve/deny query excluded. The missingness audit could not see this because nothing was blank. A **separation audit** caught it: it flags any category where only one outcome ever occurs. The leak had inflated ROC-AUC (0.799 → 0.789 once removed). It had also made automation look **more than 13× more viable** than it is: 12.2% vs 0.9% of applications at a 2% error budget (both measured on the test year, for comparison).

## Finding 2: the model is useful, with a ceiling

| Model (trained 2022, tested 2023) | ROC-AUC | Denial PR-AUC |
|---|---|---|
| Approve if DTI ≤ 43% (the textbook rule) | 0.614 | 0.139 |
| Logistic regression | 0.725 | 0.405 |
| **XGBoost, monotonic (chosen)** | **0.789** | **0.537** |
| XGBoost, unconstrained | 0.799 | 0.556 |

I chose the **monotonic** model and gave up 0.010 AUC for a guarantee the unconstrained model lacks: more debt, more leverage or less income can never *raise* approval. It is well calibrated (expected calibration error **0.003**: its probabilities match observed approval rates), and its top factor, debt-to-income, matches the lenders' own most common denial reason (39% of denials).

The model never denies anyone. It **auto-approves or refers to a person**. I set the cut-off on 2022 so that at most 5% of auto-approvals would be ones the lender denied. On 2023 it automated **69.2%** of applications at **4.9%** wrong, so the policy held. HMDA has no credit scores, and credit history and incomplete applications cause 24% of denials, so no threshold achieves a 2% budget with useful automation.

## Finding 3: "fairer on average" is not fair at the threshold

From financial features alone, the model reproduces about two-thirds of the lenders' Black–White approval gap: **−6.2 points vs −9.8**. The rest is not explained by the variables available here. That is not proof of discrimination, because credit scores are missing. But averages hide the decision. At the operating threshold, **Black applicants whom the lender approved were 21.7 points more likely to be referred for manual review** instead of auto-approved. A small shift in average scores becomes a large one at a cut-off.

| Change (Georgia 2023) | Black referral gap | ROC-AUC |
|---|---|---|
| Base model | +21.7 pp | 0.789 |
| Add census-tract features | **+30.7 pp** (geography is a proxy for race) | 0.796 |
| Reweigh training data by race × outcome | **+17.7 pp** | 0.786 |

## Finding 4: it generalises, and so does the problem

- **Over time.** Between 2021 and 2023, applicants' median debt-to-income ratio rose from 38% to 42%. A model trained on 2021 and never updated drifted just past its budget (5.2–5.3% wrong auto-approvals); the yearly retrained model stayed within it. Conclusion: retrain every year and monitor the realised error.
- **Across states.** Applied unchanged, the Georgia model came within about 0.02 AUC of models trained in each state, and kept wrong auto-approvals at 3.0–3.8%.
- **The fairness finding replicated in every state.** The Black–White referral gap was +12.8 to +24.0 points and the Hispanic gap +8.6 to +18.6. It is a property of thresholding these scores, not a Georgia quirk.

## Shipping it

The v2 model now runs in the LoanWise app. The API turns a form submission into features with the **same code** the model was trained with, and parity tests prove the two match, including HMDA's banded debt-to-income encoding. The design follows the findings: geography is excluded, a low score means review by a loan officer rather than denial, the referral letter has its own guardrail so it can never read as an approval or a refusal, and the fairness gap at the threshold is shown next to every decision instead of only in a report. 134 backend and 83 UI tests run in CI, and the API ships as a Docker image.

## What I would do next

Evaluate threshold policies that bound the referral gap directly, and make these checks release gates in CI. Then add loan-performance data with credit scores (Freddie Mac) to model repayment alongside approval.
